questions.question: How does the JVM decide that an object can be collected?
options: It cannot be reached from any GC root
It has not been used for 60 seconds
Its reference count is exactly one
Its class has a finalize() method
questions.explanation: The collector traces from GC roots. Any object with no path from a root is garbage, whatever its age or references.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a GC root?
options: A local variable of a running method
A static field of a loaded class
A field of an object that nothing references
questions.explanation: Fields of an unreachable object are not roots. Roots are stack variables, static fields, live threads and native references.

questions.question: What does System.gc() do?
options: Frees all unused objects at once
Deletes the object passed to it
Stops the program until memory is free
Requests a collection, which the JVM may run later or ignore
questions.explanation: System.gc() is only a hint. The JVM decides whether and when to collect, and it can be disabled with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC.

questions.question: Where are newly created objects usually allocated?
questions.explanation: New objects go into Eden. Survivors of minor collections move to survivor spaces and later to the old generation.

questions.question: Order a = new Order(); Order b = a; a = null; How many objects are eligible for GC right after these lines?
questions.explanation: b still refers to the Order object, so it stays reachable. Setting a to null removed only one of its two references.

questions.question: Hall h = new Hall("A"); h = new Hall("B"); h = new Hall("C"); How many Hall objects are eligible for GC after these lines?
questions.explanation: Each reassignment drops the previous object. Halls A and B have no reference left; only C is reachable through h.

questions.question: Seat x = new Seat(); Seat y = new Seat(); x.next = y; y.next = x; x = null; y = null; How many Seat objects are eligible?
options: Zero, because they refer to each other
questions.explanation: The two seats form an island of isolation. They point at each other but no root reaches them, so both are eligible.

questions.question: A service adds every request object to a static List and never removes them. Memory keeps growing. Why doesn't GC help?
options: Static lists are stored on the stack
The static field is a GC root, so every object in the list stays reachable
questions.explanation: Reachable objects are never collected. Remove entries when done or use a bounded cache.

questions.question: A class closes its file inside finalize(). Sometimes the file stays open for a long time. What is the problem?
options: finalize() runs on the main thread
Files cannot be closed by objects
finalize() may run late or never, and is deprecated; use try-with-resources
questions.explanation: Finalization depends on when GC runs, which is unpredictable. try-with-resources closes the file at a known point.

questions.question: Which garbage collector is the default in modern JDKs such as Java 11 and 17 on typical server machines?
questions.explanation: G1 became the default in Java 9. It splits the heap into regions and aims for short, predictable pauses.
